pr_body:
- The string argument in the single-argument overload should be nullable.
- All overloads on Windows should allow a null file path, but they've been throwing an exception
- On Linux, data was silently truncated when sending a file larger than int.MaxValue with BeginSendFile.

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/42530
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/42529
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/41906

issue_context.title: Socket.SendFile(string) argument is supposed to be nullable
issue_context.body: The docs for Socket.SendFile(string) state that the string argument is allowed to be null, and on .NET Framework when it's null, the operation executes fine, sending nothing.  However, in .NET 5 the string argument is annotated as non-nullable, and on Windows it throws an exception when null is provided, as in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/42529.

I could see that it can be null if you can also pass in buffer but what do you expect to happen if you use overload just with the string name and that is not provided?

The same thing that happens on .NET Framework or if you use Socket.Send(new byte[0])... it sends nothing.  I agree there's relatively little use in this, but it enables consistency with the SendFile overload that takes pre/post-buffers as well, and where null for the file stream makes more sense.

review_comments: I thought we decided in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/32675#discussion_r382830596 that this should be non-null. Calling `SendFile(null)` won't do anything, so the assumption is you should pass in a fileName.
If we are moving this to be nullable, to be consistent, we should annotate the `BeginSendFile` overload as nullable as well.

We did, but issuing a warning doesn't actually solve any problems here, and it leads to an inconsistency with the other overload.  It's not harmful to pass null, it's always been allowed on .NET Framework, etc., so we may as well gain the consistency, avoid potential noisy warnings, and allow null.

> If we are moving this to be nullable, to be consistent, we should annotate the BeginSendFile overload as nullable as well.

I thought I did.  I'll fix it.
(The docs are also explicit about null being allowed.)
Maybe a dumb question, but is there no better way to deal with a possibly null handle than to do it manually? Seems like we should be able to pass null or some special SafeHandle value here...

Not that I'm aware of.  It's pretty explicit:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/e489111db3cb25a7ff9640c2e3a6e9561f56cc07/src/coreclr/src/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/StubHelpers.cs#L1251-L1256
cc: @AaronRobinsonMSFT, @jkoritzinsky
I can understand why null is not supported, but it seems like it would be straightforward to define something like SafeHandle.ZeroHandle or whatever that always just passes a zero handle.
I just want a way to pass a zero handle without having to remove the SafeHandle from the p/invoke call and do the addref/release manually, because this is fragile.

> it seems like it would be straightforward to define something like SafeHandle.ZeroHandle or whatever that always just passes a zero handle

In most P/Invokes I've seen, as is the case here, the DllImport is strongly-typed to the SafeHandle-derived type, so you'd need to have such a ZeroHandle on each one.  (Lots of SafeHandles also consider 0 to be an invalid handle value, though I don't think that'd be an issue for this particular use case.)

In this case, we could of course create a SafeFileHandle for zero and cache it.  I'm just not sure it's worthwhile for this one use.

> Is the thought here we should let the caller pass null?

Yeah, I think that'd be useful; seems clear-cut what it means, and I'm not sure what situation throwing prevents/helps.  This isn't the first time I've seen this, though generally I've seen it manifest as someone defining two different DllImport overloads, one that takes IntPtr and one that takes SafeHandle, to work around this.  In fact that's what the equivalent code in .NET Framework does here (which we regressed at some point, leading to this fix).
@geoffkizer or @stephentoub  Feel free to file an issue for this. I think it warrants a serious discussion because I agree this is annoying.
Opened https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/42550. Thanks.
